title: 'Her word remained unwinged' (apteros mythos)
greek: τῇ δ᾽ ἄπτερος ἔπλετο μῦθος (tēi d' apteros epleto mythos)
short: The reverse of 'winged words': Penelope hears her son's instruction and makes no reply, obeying in silence.
body: The phrase plays on the familiar formula 'winged words' (epea pteroenta), which describes words actually spoken, sent flying from the speaker to the hearer. A word that is 'unwinged' (apteros, 'without wings') is therefore one that never leaves the lips. Ancient and some modern interpreters took it to mean that the speech 'stuck' in the hearer's mind; Monro argues, from the sense of the positive formula, that it must mean simply that she heard and said nothing. Here Penelope, who has just been told to bathe and vow hecatombs rather than to question her son, obeys without a word. The line occurs only in the second half of the poem and always of a woman taking an order in silence: Penelope here, Eurycleia at 19.29 and 21.386, and Eurycleia again at 22.398. It marks the moments when the household quietly falls into line behind Telemachus and Odysseus.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 17.57

title: The fountain of Ithacus, Neritus and Polyctor
greek: τὴν ποίησ᾽ Ἴθακος καὶ Νήριτος ἠδὲ Πολύκτωρ (tēn poiēs' Ithakos kai Nēritos ēde Polyktōr)
short: The town fountain was built by the island's legendary founders, eponymous heroes of Ithaca and of its mountain Neritus.
body: The spring on the road into town is a little landscape of Ithacan memory: a stone basin, a ring of poplars, cold water from the rock, and an altar of the Nymphs at which every passer-by makes an offering. Its makers are names drawn from the island itself. Ithacus is the eponym of Ithaca, Neritus of the island's wooded mountain (Od. 9.21-2; Il. 2.632), and Polyctor ('much-possessing') recurs as the father of the suitor Peisander (18.299). Monro reports the early mythographer Acusilaus, for whom the three brothers founded first Cephallenia and then Ithaca, and suggests that they belong to an older layer of local heroes partly displaced by the family of Laertes in epic tradition. The setting is pointed: at this sacred, civic place, where the Nymphs receive gifts from all comers, the goatherd Melanthius kicks a beggar. The violation of hospitality begins at a shrine.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 17.207

title: Melanthius (Melantheus), son of Dolius
greek: υἱὸς Δολίοιο Μελανθεύς (huios Dolioio Melantheus)
short: The disloyal goatherd, a 'black' name like his sister Melantho's; his abuse of the beggar marks him for the most savage punishment in the poem.
body: The goatherd appears here as Melantheus and more often as Melanthius; both, Monro notes, are shortened forms of a name built on melas, 'black', shared by his sister Melantho (18.321). Their father Dolius is the faithful old servant of Penelope and Laertes (4.735-7; 24.386-411), so the household's loyalty is divided within a single slave family. Melanthius is the exact counterpart of Eumaeus: both are herdsmen bringing animals to town, but one feeds the suitors and the other protects the stranger. His insults, his kick and his wish that Telemachus might die (17.251-3) are repaid in Book XXII, where he fetches arms for the suitors (22.135-46) and is mutilated in the courtyard (22.474-7). Steiner draws attention to the spatial markers that stage the encounter (17.182-260).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 17.212
Deborah Steiner, Homer: Odyssey Books XVII and XVIII (Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics; Cambridge, 2010), notes on 17.182-260 (p. 103), as summarised in B. Spence, BMCR 2011.04.58

title: 'The vile leads the vile': like to like
greek: κακὸς κακὸν ἡγηλάζει, ὡς αἰεὶ τὸν ὁμοῖον ἄγει θεὸς ὡς τὸν ὁμοῖον (kakos kakon hēgēlazei, hōs aiei ton homoion agei theos hōs ton homoion)
short: Melanthius' sneer uses a proverb, 'God always brings like to like', that later Greek philosophers quoted when they discussed friendship.
body: The rare verb hēgēlazei, 'plays the guide', has a contemptuous ring (Monro renders it 'plays fugleman to'): the swineherd is leading his own kind. The second line turns the insult into a proverb. Monro, following Ridgeway, takes the two words hōs as correlatives ('as god brings one, so he always brings his like') rather than treating the second as a preposition. Plato quotes the line in the Lysis (214a) when Socrates asks whether friendship is a matter of like loving like, and the idea became a commonplace of ancient ethics. The irony here is that the proverb is truer than Melanthius knows: the 'vile' pair are a loyal servant and his disguised master, and the god who brings them together is Athena.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 17.217 and 17.218

title: Scraps, not swords or cauldrons
greek: αἰτίζων ἀκόλους, οὐκ ἄορας οὐδὲ λέβητας (aitizōn akolous, ouk aoras oude lebētas)
short: Swords and tripod-cauldrons were the gifts and prizes of heroes; the beggar asks only for crusts (akoloi).
body: Melanthius' contrast measures the beggar against the world of heroic exchange. Bronze cauldrons (lebētes) and swords are what nobles give one another as guest-gifts and what heroes win as prizes: Akhilleus sets out cauldrons and tripods for the funeral games (Il. 23.259), and Menelaus and the Phaeacians load Odysseus and Telemachus with metal treasures (Od. 4.590-2, 13.13-14). The akolos is the smallest unit of food, a morsel or crust. The insult therefore places Odysseus at the bottom of the scale of gift-giving that his own adventures have taken him to the top of; the treasures the Phaeacians gave him lie hidden in a cave on this very island (13.366-71). Monro discusses the form aora (accusative of aor, 'sword') here.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 17.222

title: Odysseus endures (the first of the insults)
greek: ἀλλ᾽ ἐπετόλμησε, φρεσὶ δ᾽ ἔσχετο (all' epetolmēse, phresi d' escheto)
short: Kicked by Melanthius, Odysseus weighs two violent responses and chooses to endure: the pattern of restraint that governs Books XVII-XX.
body: The scene follows a typical Homeric decision: the hero 'pondered' (mermērixen) between two courses, here killing the goatherd with his staff or dashing his head on the ground, and then chooses a third, to hold back. The verb epetolmēse belongs to the family of tlēnai, 'to endure, to bear', which gives Odysseus his epithets polytlas and talasiphrōn ('much-enduring', 'of the steadfast heart'). Monro glosses the next phrase as 'mastered his impulse'. The same pattern of provocation, inner debate and self-restraint is repeated with Antinous' footstool (17.462-5), with Irus (18.90-4), with the maids (20.9-21) and with Ctesippus (20.299-302). In the Iliad strength shows itself in action; in these books of the Odyssey it shows itself in what the hero refrains from doing until the right moment.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 17.238

title: Eumaeus' prayer to the Nymphs of the spring
greek: νύμφαι κρηναῖαι, κοῦραι Διός, εἴ ποτ᾽ Ὀδυσσεὺς ... (nymphai krēnaiai, kourai Dios, ei pot' Odysseus)
short: Eumaeus prays in the standard 'if ever' form, reminding the local spring-nymphs of Odysseus' past sacrifices and asking for his return.
body: The Nymphs are minor goddesses of springs, woods and caves, called 'daughters of Zeus' as in the Iliad (6.420). On Ithaca they have a special place: Odysseus prays to them in their cave on landing (13.355-60). Eumaeus uses the classic structure of Greek prayer seen in Chryses' prayer to Apollo (Il. 1.37-42): an invocation, a reminder of past offerings ('if ever Odysseus burned thigh-pieces wrapped in fat'), and a request based on that relationship of exchange. His wish is fulfilled before his eyes without his knowing it, since the master he prays for is standing beside him. The prayer also sets piety against impiety at the same altar: the herdsman remembers what is owed to the gods, while Melanthius forgets what is owed to strangers.

title: The belly (gastēr)
greek: γαστέρα δ᾽ οὔ πως ἔστιν ἀποκρύψαι μεμαυῖαν (gastera d' ou pōs estin apokrypsai memauian)
short: Odysseus' disguise forces him to speak as a beggar, ruled by the 'accursed' belly that drives men to beg, steal and even to war.
body: In the beggar's role Odysseus repeatedly blames the gastēr, the hungry stomach, as a tyrant over human beings: it cannot be hidden, it brings many evils, and for its sake ships are fitted out to raid enemies overseas (17.286-9; compare 7.215-21, 15.344-5, 17.473-4, 18.53-4). The theme has two edges. It is the humiliating truth of poverty that the suitors, who consume another man's livelihood, never feel; and it is also a darker comment on heroic warfare, which here appears as plunder for the sake of food. The belly thus becomes in the Odyssey an emblem of the need that binds the hero to the human condition, in contrast to the Iliadic warrior's apparent indifference to food. Hesiod's Muses mock shepherds as 'mere bellies' (Theogony 26), and Book XVIII will literally make Odysseus fight for a stuffed paunch.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 17.286

title: Argos, the old hound
greek: Ἄργος, Ὀδυσσῆος ταλασίφρονος (Argos, Odyssēos talasiphronos)
short: The first creature in the palace to recognise Odysseus is his old dog, who wags his tail, drops his ears, and dies 'in the twentieth year'.
body: Argos' name is the adjective argos, 'swift' or 'flashing', used of hounds already in the Iliad (kunes argoi, 1.50). Bred by Odysseus but never enjoyed by him, he once hunted wild goats, deer and hares; now he lies neglected on the dung-heap before the doors, full of ticks. His state mirrors his master's and the household's: beauty and strength degraded by twenty years of absence and by servants who no longer care (17.318-23). The recognition is wordless and instant, the reverse of every later recognition, which must be tested and earned. Odysseus can only turn aside and wipe away a tear unseen. The closing line, in which death takes the dog 'when he had seen Odysseus in the twentieth year', fixes the length of the absence and gives the scene its famous restraint. Steiner devotes an extended note to the episode's pathos and to its likeness to divine epiphany.

sources.cite: Deborah Steiner, Homer: Odyssey Books XVII and XVIII (Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics; Cambridge, 2010), notes on 17.291-327 (pp. 116-18), as summarised in B. Spence, BMCR 2011.04.58
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 17.306-327

title: Table-dogs (trapezēes kunes)
greek: τραπεζῆες κύνες ἀνδρῶν (trapezēes kunes andrōn)
short: Dogs kept by the master's table for show, as opposed to working hounds: Odysseus' feigned question draws out Eumaeus' praise of Argos.
body: Monro glosses trapezēes as 'fed from the table'. The term comes from the Iliad, where the table-dogs belong to great households: Priam imagines his own table-dogs devouring his corpse at the gate (Il. 22.66-71), and Akhilleus throws two of Patroclus' nine table-dogs on the funeral pyre (Il. 23.173). Odysseus pretends not to know whether Argos is a hunting dog or a mere ornament, and the question prompts Eumaeus to describe the dog in his prime, unbeatable in the chase and keen of scent. The exchange is typical of the disguised hero's method in these books: he asks, as a stranger, questions to which he knows the answer, and so tests the loyalty and memory of the person who replies.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 17.309

title: Zeus takes half a man's worth on 'the day of slavery'
greek: ἥμισυ γάρ τ᾽ ἀρετῆς ἀποαίνυται εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς ἀνέρος, εὖτ᾽ ἄν μιν κατὰ δούλιον ἦμαρ ἕλῃσιν (hēmisu gar t' aretēs apoainutai euruopa Zeus aneros, eut' an min kata doulion ēmar helēisin)
short: Eumaeus' saying on slavery, quoted by Plato, explains the maids' neglect; it is spoken by a man who was himself born free and sold.
body: Arete here is not yet 'virtue' in the later moral sense; Monro takes it broadly as a man's 'good' or worth. 'The day of slavery' (doulion ēmar) is a formula of the Iliad, where Hector imagines Andromache led away by an Achaean, robbed of her 'day of freedom' (Il. 6.455-63). Plato quotes these lines in the Laws (777a) in a discussion of the management of slaves, with the variant 'half of his mind' (noos), a reading Monro judges less Homeric than the vulgate. The saying gains force from its speaker: Eumaeus was a king's son, kidnapped as a child by Phoenician traders and sold to Laertes (15.403-84). His explanation of why the women neglect Argos is therefore also, unawares, a comment on his own life and on the loyalty that he has kept in spite of it.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 17.322 and 17.322-3 (with the text of Plato, Laws 777a)

title: The ashen threshold (meilinos oudos)
greek: ἷζε δ᾽ ἐπὶ μελίνου οὐδοῦ ἔντοσθε θυράων (hize d' epi melinou oudou entosthe thuraōn)
short: Odysseus takes the beggar's place on the threshold of his own hall, the spot from which he will later shoot the suitors.
body: The palace has more than one threshold: a 'stone threshold' at the entrance (17.30, 20.258) and this ash-wood one inside the doorway of the hall. Monro discusses their relation in his appendix on the Homeric house and notes that the adjective, elsewhere meilinos, is used here in the form melinos. The threshold is the proper station of the beggar, who sits neither outside nor among the feasters. It becomes a charged space in the following books: Odysseus and Irus quarrel over it ('this threshold will hold us both', 18.17), Telemachus seats his father there (20.257-9), and in Book XXII Odysseus leaps onto the great threshold with bow and arrows to begin the slaughter (22.1-4). The place of humiliation is also the place of command.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 17.339 and Appendix on the Homeric House

title: Aidōs: 'shame is no good companion for a man in need'
greek: αἰδὼς δ᾽ οὐκ ἀγαθὴ κεχρημένῳ ἀνδρὶ παρεῖναι (aidōs d' ouk agathē kechrēmenōi andri pareinai)
short: Telemachus sends his 'guest' to beg, invoking a proverb about aidōs (shame, respect) that Hesiod also knows.
body: Aidōs is the sense of shame or respect that holds a person back in the presence of others: before elders, gods, guests or public opinion. For a man in need it becomes a handicap, since it stops him from asking. Hesiod gives almost the same saying in the Works and Days (317-19), where 'aidōs is no good guide for a needy man'. The proverb recurs in reverse when Penelope says that a beggar who feels shame is a bad beggar (17.578), and Monro there notes the personal construction ('it is bad for a wanderer to be aidoios'). The word cuts both ways in these books. The beggar must lay aside aidōs; the suitors, by contrast, are condemned for having none, 'no share of aidōs in their hearts' (20.171). Douglas Cairns' study of the concept traces its role as the central social emotion of Homeric ethics.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 17.578
Douglas L. Cairns, Aidōs: The Psychology and Ethics of Honour and Shame in Ancient Greek Literature (Oxford, 1993)

title: Athena's test: 'righteous and lawless'
greek: γνοίη θ᾽ οἵ τινές εἰσιν ἐναίσιμοι οἵ τ᾽ ἀθέμιστοι (gnoiē th' hoi tines eisin enaisimoi hoi t' athemistoi)
short: Athena sends Odysseus begging to sort the just suitors from the lawless, yet the narrator adds at once that none will be spared.
body: Enaisimos means 'in accordance with what is due' (aisa), athemistos 'without themis', outside the order of right. The begging round is thus framed as a moral test, like a god visiting mortals to see their hospitality. But the next line closes the question: 'yet even so she was not minded to save one of them from ruin'. Monro notes that the verb (mellō) here signals destiny rather than intention: she 'was not going to' spare any. The tension is deliberate and much discussed. The poem insists on the suitors' collective guilt, yet it also shows decent individuals among them, above all Amphinomus (18.119-57), who are doomed with the rest. Steiner places this within the books' wider theodicy, the attempt to show that the coming revenge is just.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 17.364

Deborah Steiner, Homer: Odyssey Books XVII and XVIII (Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics; Cambridge, 2010), Introduction (hospitality, theoxeny and the ethics of revenge), as summarised in B. Spence, BMCR 2011.04.58

title: Going round 'on the right' (endexia)
greek: βῆ δ᾽ ἴμεν αἰτήσων ἐνδέξια φῶτα ἕκαστον (bē d' imen aitēsōn endexia phōta hekaston)
short: Odysseus begs from left to right round the hall, the lucky direction used for serving wine and for taking turns.
body: Endexia means 'from left to right', in the direction of the right hand, which the Greeks regarded as auspicious. In the Iliad Hephaestus pours nectar for the gods 'from left to right' (Il. 1.597), and in Book XXI Antinous proposes that the suitors try the bow in the same order, 'beginning from the place where the wine is poured' (21.141-2). By following the order of the feast, Odysseus behaves as a proper participant in the banquet rather than an intruder, which makes the suitors' treatment of him the more shameful. The begging round also gives the narrative a structure: the reader meets the suitors one by one until the round reaches Antinous.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 18.425 (serving 'in succession')

title: Dēmioergoi: workers for the people
greek: δημιοεργοὶ ... μάντιν ἢ ἰητῆρα κακῶν ἢ τέκτονα δούρων, ἢ καὶ θέσπιν ἀοιδόν (dēmioergoi ... mantin ē iētēra kakōn ē tektona dourōn, ē kai thespin aoidon)
short: Eumaeus lists the wandering specialists men invite from abroad: seer, healer, builder, and the divine singer.
body: Dēmioergos (later dēmiourgos, the word Plato uses for the divine craftsman) means one who works 'for the people', not for his own household. Monro glosses 'workers for the common weal', in contrast to farmers or merchants who deal only with their own goods; at 19.135 the word is applied to heralds 'whose trade is a public one'. Eumaeus' list is a valuable glimpse of early Greek society, in which skilled men travel from community to community and are welcomed for their art. The presence of the singer among them is the poet quietly naming his own profession, and the comparison is soon turned on Odysseus himself, whose tales enchant Eumaeus 'as when a man gazes upon a minstrel' (17.518-21). A beggar, Eumaeus insists, belongs to no such class: nobody invites him.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 17.383

anchor: seized the footstool and flung it
title: Antinous' footstool: the first of three missiles
greek: θρῆνυν ἑλὼν βάλε δεξιὸν ὦμον (thrēnun helōn bale dexion ōmon)
short: Antinous hurls a footstool at the beggar, the first of three objects thrown by suitors at Odysseus (17.462, 18.394, 20.299).
body: Melanthius had predicted that footstools would be broken on the beggar's ribs (17.231-2), a joke Monro calls a piece of rough humour. Antinous fulfils it: the stool (thrēnus) on which he rests his feet strikes Odysseus at the base of the right shoulder, 'full in the back' as Monro explains, yet he stands 'firm as a rock'. The pattern then repeats with variation: Eurymachus throws a stool but hits the wine-pourer (18.394-8), and Ctesippus throws an ox-hoof, which Odysseus dodges (20.299-302). Each scene escalates the outrage, and each thrower dies in the order of his offence: Antinous first (22.8-21), Eurymachus second (22.79-88), and Ctesippus with a taunt that recalls his 'gift' (22.285-91). The wooers themselves sense the danger (17.483-7).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 17.231-2 and 17.463

title: The Egyptian tale and 'a bitter Egypt'
greek: μὴ τάχα πικρὴν Αἴγυπτον καὶ Κύπρον ἵκηαι (mē tacha pikrēn Aigupton kai Kupron hikēai)
short: Odysseus retells his false Cretan-Egyptian story to Antinous, who answers with a sarcastic oxymoron.
body: The beggar's story of a raid on Egypt that went wrong (17.419-44) repeats, almost line for line, the lie Odysseus told Eumaeus (14.258-72), as Monro notes; here he ends it with a new detail, a fictitious Dmetor, son of Iasus, king of Cyprus. Such 'Cretan lies' are a feature of the second half of the poem: each blends true experience (shipwreck, lost comrades, the danger of plundering) with invented identities, and each is tailored to its listener. To the arrogant Antinous the moral is clear: a rich man lost everything through his men's violence. Antinous replies with an oxymoron, 'a bitter Egypt', meaning, as Monro puts it, something quite unlike Egypt; the phrase parallels 'bitter marriage' (pikrogamoi, 17.137), used of the suitors themselves.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 17.427-41 and 17.448

title: The Erinyes of beggars
greek: ἀλλ᾽ εἴ που πτωχῶν γε θεοὶ καὶ Ἐρινύες εἰσίν (all' ei pou ptōchōn ge theoi kai Erinyes eisin)
short: Odysseus curses Antinous by the Erinyes, spirits who avenge those with no human protector: here the beggar.
body: The Erinyes (Murray's 'avengers') are powers who punish wrongs that no human court can reach, especially offences against parents (Il. 9.454, 9.571; Od. 2.135, 11.280). Here the idea is extended to the destitute. The beggar has no kin to avenge him, so he appeals to the gods who protect strangers and suppliants: 'all strangers and beggars are from Zeus' (6.207-8; 14.57-8), and Zeus is 'the avenger of suppliants and strangers' (9.270-1). Odysseus' curse that Antinous may die 'before his marriage' is fulfilled with exactness: he is the first suitor to fall, shot through the throat while lifting a wine cup (22.8-21). The curse thus links the human beggar's wrong to the divine order that the poem claims stands behind the revenge.

title: Gods disguised as strangers (theoxeny)
greek: καί τε θεοὶ ξείνοισιν ἐοικότες ἀλλοδαποῖσι, παντοῖοι τελέθοντες, ἐπιστρωφῶσι πόληας (kai te theoi xeinoisin eoikotes allodapoisi, pantoioi telethontes, epistrōphōsi poleēas)
short: A suitor warns that the beggar might be a god in disguise, since gods wander among cities testing men's violence and justice.
body: This is the clearest statement in Homer of the belief behind theoxeny, the story-type in which a god visits mortals in humble disguise and rewards or punishes them according to their hospitality (compare the later tale of Baucis and Philemon in Ovid, Metamorphoses 8). Emily Kearns argued that the whole return of Odysseus is shaped on this pattern: the master comes home as an unrecognised stranger, tests his household, and repays each member as a visiting god would. Monro analyses the syntax as an unfinished warning ('if he is some god...'), completed by the general statement about gods 'beholding the violence and the righteousness of men'. Plato disapproved of the lines: in the Republic (381d) Socrates cites them as an example of poets' lies about the gods changing shape.

sources.cite: Emily Kearns, 'The Return of Odysseus: A Homeric Theoxeny', Classical Quarterly n.s. 32 (1982) 2-8
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 17.483 ff.

title: Odysseus as singer (the minstrel simile)
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτ᾽ ἀοιδὸν ἀνὴρ ποτιδέρκεται ... ὣς ἐμὲ κεῖνος ἔθελγε (hōs d' hot' aoidon anēr potiderketai ... hōs eme keinos ethelge)
short: Eumaeus compares the stranger's storytelling to a god-taught bard's song: Odysseus 'enchanted' (thelgein) him for three days.
body: The verb thelgein, 'to enchant, to bewitch', is used of Circe's drugs and the Sirens' song as well as of poetry; Eumaeus says Odysseus' words would 'charm thy very soul' (17.514). The simile belongs to a series in which Odysseus is likened to a poet: Alcinous praises him for telling his tale 'skilfully, as a minstrel does' (11.367-9), and when he finally strings the great bow he does it as easily as a singer stretches a string on his lyre (21.404-9). The comparison is double-edged, because the tale that enchanted Eumaeus was a lie. The Odyssey repeatedly links the power of song with the power to deceive, and its hero is master of both.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 17.514

title: Telemachus' sneeze as omen
greek: Τηλέμαχος δὲ μέγ᾽ ἔπταρεν, ἀμφὶ δὲ δῶμα σμερδαλέον κονάβησε (Tēlemachos de meg' eptaren, amphi de dōma smerdaleon konabēse)
short: A loud sneeze at the moment Penelope wishes for Odysseus' vengeance is taken as a sign that the wish will be fulfilled.
body: Greeks regarded an involuntary sneeze that coincided with a spoken wish as a sign of divine confirmation. In Xenophon's Anabasis (3.2.9), when a soldier sneezes during a speech about safety, the whole army bows to Zeus the Saviour. Penelope reads her son's sneeze in the same way and laughs, the first of several unexpected laughs in these books (compare 18.163). Monro notes the mock-heroic tone: the adverb smerdaleon ('terribly'), used in the Iliad of shields and war-cries, here describes a sneeze that makes the house ring. The scene is light, but it is one of a chain of omens in Books XVII-XX (the bird-sign of Theoclymenus, the kledones of 18.117 and 20.100-21, Zeus' thunder) that point to the suitors' destruction.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 17.542

anchor: like unto Artemis or golden Aphrodite
title: Penelope 'like Artemis or golden Aphrodite'
greek: Ἀρτέμιδι ἰκέλη ἠὲ χρυσέῃ Ἀφροδίτῃ (Artemidi ikelē ēe chruseēi Aphroditēi)
short: A double comparison that joins the virgin huntress and the goddess of desire: chastity and attraction held together in Penelope.
body: Comparisons of a beautiful woman to a goddess are common in Homer (Nausicaa is like Artemis, 6.102-9, 6.151; Helen comes forth 'like Artemis of the golden arrow', 4.122). The paired line used here, and again at 19.54, is unusual in joining two goddesses of opposite character. Artemis stands for virginity and for women's protected status; Aphrodite for erotic power and marriage. The pairing suits the situation of Books XVII-XIX, where Penelope remains faithful yet is about to show herself to the suitors and consider remarriage. It also anticipates her own prayers: she calls on Artemis to grant her a gentle death (18.202-5; 20.61-90), while Athena beautifies her with the cosmetic of Aphrodite (18.192-4).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), critical note on 17.37 (ἠὲ vs. ἠδὲ)
